285.dq: Final stress avoidance results in a stress lapse at the right edge of a word containing an odd number of syllables. Languages displaying this type of stress lapse at the right periphery include Pintupi (Hansen and Hansen 1969, 1978) ... stress on odd-numbered non-final syllables counting from the left (Hansen and Hansen 1969, 1978). Examples of stress in Pintupi appear in (24). a. tjútaja 'many' …

285.prule: Primary stress falls on the initial syllable of the phonological word; the one stated exception is a word beginning with the change-of-subject morpheme ka (possible only after pause, directly before a stem), which takes primary stress on its second syllable (Hansen & Hansen 1969:161-162).
285.srule: Secondary stress is optional and noncontrastive: in fast speech words carry only primary stress; in slower speech words of more than three syllables may carry a secondary stress on the third syllable (4-5 syllables), the third and fifth (6-7), the third, fifth and seventh (8-9), never the final syllable (Hansen & Hansen 1969:161-162). Relay works (Gordon 2002, Heinz 2023, Stanton 2014) restate this as categorical 'secondary stress on non-final odd syllables'.
285.quote: One subtype of these ‘binary plus lapse’ systems is found in languages in which stress falls on odd-numbered syllables from left to right except for final syllables, e.g., σ́σσ̀σσ, σ́σσ̀σσ̀σ. Final stress avoidance results in a stress lapse at the right edge of a word containing an odd number of syllables. Languages displaying this type of stress lapse at the right periphery include Pintupi (Hansen and Hansen 1969, 1978) and Karelian (Leskinen 1984). [...] We now look more closely at the constraint-based analysis of the binary plus external lapse system found in Pintupi: stress on odd-numbere…

285.exq_: When the morpheme ka 'change of subj. indicator' occurs in the initial position of the phonological word, primary stress falls on the second syllable of that word. The morpheme ka is word initial only when it follows pause and contiguously precedes a stem

morph.rootq: "Primary lexical stress occurs on the first syllable. Usually, Western Desert languages are described as having secondary stress on odd numbered syllables following primary stress (with no stress on final syllables); however phonetic investigations into the closely-related Pitjantjatjara have concluded that there is no evidence for secondary stress, contra wide-spread claims to the contrary (Tabain et al., 2014)." (Gray 2024: 39, §2.1). Footnote 3: "As Wilmoth (2022) notes though, there are morphological complexities surrounding stress placement that were not taken into account by Tabain et al. (2014)." Also fn.13 p.101, citing Hansen & Hansen (2022): the bound -wiya "does not receive…
morph.elicq: "This section is largely based on descriptions in Hansen and Hansen (1969) and Hansen and Hansen (1978), and is similar to descriptions of the phonetics and phonology of other Western Desert languages ... until now only Pitjantjatjara has been the subject of detailed phonetic investigations" (Gray 2024: 38, §2.1). The stress statement is second-hand from Hansen & Hansen; the only instrumental work cited (Tabain et al. 2014) is on Pitjantjatjara, not Pintupi-Luritja, and Gray adds that the stress difference between bound and free wiya "awaits detailed study" (fn.13, p.101).
morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing and encliticising: "Pintupi-Luritja on the whole exhibits... agglutinating morphology, dependent marking, a person-based split-ergative case marking system, a series of second position clitics that cross-reference clausal arguments" (p.37); "Verbs are inflected in an agglutinating fashion: inflectional markers are realised as suffixes that attach to the verb stem" (p.71); "case markers appear at the right edge of the nominal they mark" (p.52); no prefixes of any kind appear in the description or examples.

evidence_works.detail: Stress is on the first syllable with no secondary stress, as the catalog entry already states from Tabain, Fletcher & Butcher 2014. The article adds consonantal correlates: under stress the bursts of /c/ and /k/ lengthen, /k/ becomes darker (lower centre of gravity) and the initial apical becomes lighter, while apical bursts do not lengthen.

evidence_works.detail: Primary stress: fixed on the first syllable of each word, one rhythmic foot per word of 2-3 syllables, stressed+unstressed -- confirms the catalog rule (10 100 1000...). Secondary stress: the parenthesis 'Multisyllabic suffixes may also have their own foot' implies a second foot (a further stress) on polysyllabic suffixes, which is in tension with the catalog's sec_status 'stated: none (one stress per word)' from Tabain & Butcher 2014; Rose does not say 'secondary stress' explicitly and gives no examples of it. No weight sensitivity, no exceptions, no vowel length stated. 'Tone' in this work

sources.text: "Each word pronounced in isolation is marked by a stress on the initial syllable. The remaining syllables of a disyllabic or trisyllabic word are not as weak as unstressed syllables are in English. ... In words of more than two syllables, there is a tendency for a secondary stress to appear. It normally appears on the third syllable of words of four syllables. 287.dq: Place primary stress on the first syllable of every word, and secondary stress on the first syllable of every polysyllabic morpheme that is not the first. if a non-initial polysyllabic morpheme is preceded by a monosyllabic morpheme, the stress may be optionally advanced to this monosyllable. Secondary stress falls on alternates, but not on the last (Blake & Green 1971:32)

287.srule: Weak secondary stress tends to appear in words of more than two syllables: normally on the third syllable of a four-syllable word; where a new morpheme begins at the fourth syllable of a five-syllable word it falls there instead (ṭakuku-inu) (Blake 1979:191). StressTyp2, digesting Blake & Breen 1971:32, generalises: secondary stress on the first syllable of each non-initial polysyllabic morpheme (optionally advanced onto a preceding monosyllabic morpheme), otherwise on alternate syllables after the primary, never on the last.
287.quote: Each word pronounced in isolation is marked by a stress on the initial syllable. The remaining syllables of a disyllabic or trisyllabic word are not as weak as unstressed syllables are in English. ... In words of more than two syllables, there is a tendency for a secondary stress to appear. It normally appears on the third syllable of words of four syllables. In a word of five syllables where a new morpheme begins in the fourth syllable, the secondary stress appears in the fourth syllable, ṯákuku-ìnu. The secondary stress is quite weak.

289.prule: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, in inflected and derived words alike, so it moves rightward under suffixation (reporter, reporter+a, reporter+owi, reporter+sk+iego); a lexically marked set of nouns has antepenultimate stress in certain inflected forms (gramatyka, uniwersytet), as do the numerals 400-900.
289.srule: Rhythmic secondary stresses alternate left to right starting with a beat on the word-initial syllable, never adjacent to the penultimate primary (X x X x, X x x X x, X x X x X x); Rubach & Booij state they are all optional (slow, careful speech only; internal ones level before the initial one) and are computed over the phonological phrase, not the word.
289.quote: As is well known, primary stress in Polish falls on the penult both in inflected stems and in derived words. Therefore its place changes under suffixation: (1) reporter 'reporter' (nom.sg.): reporter + a (gen.sg.), reporter+owi (dat. sg.) ..., reporter+sk+i (Adj., nom.sg.), reporter+ sk + iego (Adj., gen. sg.), etc. [...] It is also well known that in some cases Polish has an antepenultimate main stress. These cases are discussed in section 3 under the heading 'Extrametricality'.

morph.rootq: Swan 2002:20: 'Stress in a Polish word is fixed and predictable; it falls on the next-to-last syllable: sprawa SPRA-wa ... When a word is extended by multisyllablic suffixes or endings, the stress shifts accordingly to the right: kobieta ko-BIE-ta woman, kobietami ko-bie-TA-mi-Ipl., czytam CZY-tam I read, czytają czy-TA-ją they read. Only a few instances violate this general rule: a. Enclitics such as the past-tense personal endings -śmy and -ście and the conditional particle by do not, in standard Polish, cause the stress to shift to the right: znali ZNA-li they knew, znaliśmy ZNA-li-śmy we knew'. Same in Feldstein & Franks 2002:19 ('words are stressed on the next to last syllable') and…
morph.elicq: Swan 2002 and Feldstein & Franks 2002 give no statement of the evidence basis (unstated; Feldstein cites Wierzchowska 1967 for phonetics). The stress source behind our coding, Rubach & Booij 1985:284-285: 'The data used in this paper are drawn in part from Dłuska ((1957) and (1974)) and in part from the observations and noninstrumental experiments (lists of words, read by native speakers, etc.) carried out by one of the authors, Jerzy Rubach, who is a native speaker of Polish' (Dłuska 1974 'looks at the length of vowels', p.283). Oliver & Grice 2003 (ICPhS) is instrumental/connected speech: 'Data from 40 native speakers ... when reading a literary text. Stress was auditorily transcribed by…
morph.stmt: Predominantly suffixing: all nominal inflection (fused case-number endings), verbal person/tense endings, and derivation (diminutive -k-, verbaliser -owa-, verbal noun -nie/-cie, imperfectivising -a-/-ywa-) are suffixal; the one systematic prefixal layer is the set of perfectivising/lexical verbal prefixes (po-, u-, z-, za-, prze-, wy-, od-...), with negation nie a proclitic and się/by mobile enclitics. Feldstein & Franks 2002:4: 'Polish is marked by a complex inflectional morphology: a large inventory of grammatical forms and a significant number of stem alternations, conditioned by a wide variety of grammatical endings'; Swan 2002:374: 'Polish uses mainly (a) case endings on nouns, and…

289.sec_rule: Optional rhythmic (secondary) stresses, present in slow careful speech: binary alternation from the word-initial syllable rightward (Beat Addition, L-to-R, peak first), never adjacent to the penultimate main stress, so odd-parity words have a lapse before the penult: X x X x, X x x X x, ˌrewoˌlucjoˈnista, ˌrewoˌlucjonisˈtami, ˌkonstanˌtynoˌpoliˈtańczyk; in faster speech word-internal beats drop before the initial one (X x X x X x > X x x x X x > x x x x X x).
289.sec_quote: [p. 283] Polish has a regular pattern of alternating rhythmic stresses. [p. 284] rhythmic stresses in Polish are all optional, i.e., they are present in slow and careful speech but disappear in rapid speech. The only stress that is never affected, regardless of the tempo of speech, is the primary stress [p. 296] (27) Beat Addition (BA): Add a beat to construct a perfect grid (L-R; peak).
289.sec_cite: Rubach, Jerzy & Geert Booij (1985). A grid theory of stress in Polish. Lingua 66: 281-319.

evidence_works.measured: acoustic prominence of syllables traditionally associated with different stress levels, in simple words and compounds
evidence_works.finding: simple words show one (penultimate) prominence and no phonetic secondary stress; disagrees with Łukaszewicz 2018, which finds phonetic evidence for iterative secondary stress
evidence_works.quote: An analysis of the acoustic prominence of syllables traditionally associated with different stress levels suggests that Polish simple words exhibit only one (penultimate) prominence. The stress pattern in compounds is less uniform; they can carry one or two (penultimate) stresses, depending on their prosodic structure.

evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: The article is an L2 pedagogy pilot on English word stress in Polish learners; its only statement on Polish is a background summary (fixed penultimate primary stress, alternating secondary stress, loudness vs F0 as correlate, citing Dłuska, Weinsberg, Jassem), which agrees with the catalog's fixed-penultimate entry. Its own finding is that learners misstress English mostly by overgeneralising English rules, with penultimate transfer from Polish in only a few words (industry, cholera, Japan, event, success).

Based on classroom observation, with no measurement and no mention of tone.

Its own data are on the English of 32 Polish students, whose stress placement was judged auditorily by two raters, so nothing is measured on Polish itself.

evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: A research proposal, with no recordings or results, arguing that word-final obstruent devoicing in Polish depends on the obstruent's position in the metrical foot rather than on the following segment alone. 290.srule: Stated (McLendon 1966 §§132-133): a phonemic secondary stress /`/ (loudness without pitch shift) occurs only in a phrase that also has a primary stress; its place is lexical/morphological, not rhythmic — it is the demoted ('ablauted') primary of the second member of a compound, of a secondary verb stem, or of a verb stem after preverb xa·- (§590, §§1035-1036), and certain suffixes carry it (§230); it can contrast in position with the primary (xa·máwi·nà· vs xa·màwi·ná·). Separately, non-phonemic rhythm: every second syllable after a primary or secondary stress is slightly louder than its neighbours (§133; Buckley 2014/2019 'alternating secondary stress').

No count-only corrected pattern exists. True rule of record (Halpern 1946b:150, sec. 16): accent falls on the last vowel of any verb or noun stem regardless of its position in the word; certain nonthematic suffixes (hortatory -ú/iyú, future possible interrogative -ú·m/iyú·m) are inherently accented, so a word carries one accent (last stem vowel) or two (last stem vowel + accented suffix). Position per length is morphology-determined: attested 01 (aʔí·m), 010 (maʔéta), 00100 (kamaʔéxalʸa), plus two-accent words (aʔíyú, ʔaðúwú·m, kaná·vú) that no single-1 pattern represents.

291.srule: Placed by morphology, not rhythmic: a word has one accent (last vowel of the stem) or two; a second accent occurs only on an inherently accented nonthematic suffix after the stem (e.g. hortatory -u/-iyu, future possible interrogative -u.m/-iyu.m), and of the two the stem accent is primary and the suffix accent secondary ('When a word contains two accents, the first accent in the word is always primary... vowels in the post-accentual position may be unaccented or may bear a secondary accent'). No alternating secondary stress is described.

291.sec_quote: 6 When a word contains two accents, the first accent in the word is always primary. Thus all vowels in the pre-accentual position are unac- cented, while vowels in the post-accentual position may be unaccented or may bear a secondary accent. The vowel which bears the primary accent is in the accented position. See also 16.

morph.rootq: Sola & Parker 1964 §2.3 (p.6): 'There are two significant levels of stress in Ayacucho Quechua. Weak stress has two allophones, of which the strongest occurs on the initial syllable of words of four or more syllables. Strong stress falls on the penultimate or final syllable of the word; in the former case it is indirectly represented by space, and in the latter by the acute diacritic.' (final stress = emphatic enclitic /-Á/, §8.213: 'represented by stress shift from penultimate to final syllable'; and interjections §3.141). Zariquiey & Córdova 2008 p.34: 'Las palabras del quechua chanca siempre portan el acento en la penúltima sílaba ... conforme se añaden sufijos a una palabra, el acento…
morph.elicq: Sola & Parker 1964 ch.1 (pp.1-2) on the corpus, with no statement specific to stress: 'The principal informant, both in Peru and at Cornell, has been Mr. Alfredo Olarte Mejía ... Also, for this research Miss Jesús Ramírez ... dictated a series of folk tales recorded in her native district of Puquio, province of Lucanas. Similar texts from the province of Cangallo ... also form part of the corpus for this study.' §2.3-2.4 add only that juncture 'is often absent in rapid speech' and that for word isolability 'the native speaker is often uncertain, or speakers disagree'. No frame, wordlist or instrumental procedure is named for the stress statement.
morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing and agglutinative: Zariquiey & Córdova 2008 p.36 'el quechua es una lengua sufijal y aglutinante, lo cual quiere decir que las palabras se forman mediante la adición a la raíz de múltiples partículas llamadas terminaciones o sufijos' (llaqta-cha-yki-chik-kuna-manta-chá); Sola & Parker 1964 describe all inflection (person, number, case, aspect-tense, subordination, mood), all derivation (16 'modal suffixes', nominalizers, verbalizers) and 'thirteen bound morphemes in seven positions, following suffixes' (enclitics, §3.32) as post-root; the only pre-verbal grammatical markers are free particles (negators mana/ama, §3.146).

evidence_works.detail: Primary stress: always penultimate, predictable, shifts rightward as suffixes are added (matches catalog kind=fixed, penultimate rule). Exceptions stated: final-stressed (aguda) words with marked pragmatic value: exclamative particles in -w (alaláw, ananáw, akakáw; -y in some dialects), emphatic expressions and some questions with -rí (aripunimá, qamrí?, arí); no antepenultimate (esdrújula) words. Secondary stress: not mentioned anywhere (the catalog's alternating secondary rule is neither confirmed nor contradicted). Weight: not invoked; syllable types V, VC, CV, CVC only, no clusters within

morph.rootq: ADJUDICATED (A 'partly' -> 'no'). The rule is stated on the word in every source and suffixes sit inside the stress domain and bear stress: 'Cole (1982:208) states that IK carries stress on the penultimate syllable of the word by default' with [kal."pa.na] 'run.INF', [kal.pa."tSi.na] 'make them run' (stress on causative -chi), '[a]ffixed words such as [wa.si."tSi.na] or [kal.pa."tSi.na] ... carry the stress on the penultimate syllable' (Gualapuro 2017:43-44); 'In IQ, stress almost always falls on the penultimate syllable' (Sylak-Glassman 2013:311 fn.2); 'Stress is assigned to the penultimate syllable by default, with only few instances of last-syllable stress' (Gomez Rendon 2008:185).…
morph.elicq: Gualapuro 2017:1: 'Cole (1982:199-215) explains some phonological patterns in IK and how it differs from other varieties of Kichwa. I will follow his work, and use my own judgement as a native speaker of IK to inform this study.' 2017:43: 'IK has a simple, predictable and straightforward system. The examples in (29) and (30) indicate how stress is distributed in the syllable structure of IK.' -- tables (29)-(30) are lists of isolated citation forms transcribed by the native-speaker author (e.g. [kal."pa.na] 'run.INFINITIVE', ["wasi-mi] 'house-VAL'); no frame sentences, texts or measurements are mentioned, and he closes 'I leave a precise description of stress in IK for future research'…
morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing and agglutinative: 'It is a prototypical example of an agglutinating language... Imbabura Quichua (henceforth IQ) possesses no prefixes, and verbs containing up to nine distinct suffixes have been recorded' (Sylak-Glassman 2013:311); 'Quichua morphology is based on inflectional and derivational suffixes. The only exception is the prefix la- "in-law", albeit it does not occur in all Ecuadorian varieties' and 'Ecuadorian Quichua remains typologically identical to other Quechua languages in agglutination, suffixation and verb-final word order' (Gomez Rendon 2008:187, 191).

296.dq: K'ICHEE' STRESS GENERALIZATION: Stress falls on the final syllable of a prosodic word, unless that syllable is light non-root material, in which case it falls on the final root syllable. The first part of the generalization is that stress is attracted to the right edge of the prosodic word.

morph.rootq: Main rule is word-based, not root-based: 'Stress in Quiché always falls on the final syllable' (p.21); 'stress is not phonemic in Quiché. It is entirely predictable, falling regularly on the final syllable' (p.76). Morphology enters only via two unstressable suffix allomorphs: 'Stress in Quiché is regularly placed on the last syllable of a word in isolation. There is at least one exception to this, however. When an adjective appears before a noun that it modifies, the adjective takes a suffix -V ... Though this suffix forms part of the final syllable of the adjective under such conditions, this suffix is never stressed. Indeed, it often sounds like it is the syllable preceding this suffix…
morph.elicq: 'Stress in Quiché is regularly placed on the last syllable of a word in isolation.' (ch.2 fn.11, p.86) together with impressionistic observations on connected/phrasal speech: '[the particles wih and nah] ... are unstressed, when they appear in non phrase-final position' and 'in sentence (7a) in the text, the final /h/ is dropped in the word kaxwah because it appears in non phrase-final position ... nevertheless, the final vowel in this word is stressed' (pp.87-88). No instrumental measurements; fieldwork with PLFM Quiché-speaking linguists (Momostenango, Sta. María Chiquimula, Nahualá, Cantel).
morph.stmt: 'The primary morphological processes in Quiché are prefixation and suffixation. The vast majority of the prefixes are inflectional whereas the vast majority of the suffixes are derivational. Some of the derivational suffixes involve reduplication. Compounding is another important word-formation process' (§3.1 p.97): person marking (Set A prefixes, Set B and TAM proclitics) precedes the root; status, voice, causative, nominalising and verbalising morphology follows it.

298.quote: Metrical structure as described in §2.3.2 above allows a simple description of word stress: the final foot of the word is prominent. morph.stmt: Ritharngu is overwhelmingly suffixing: case, number, kin-possessive, tense/mood, negation (-ʔmayʔ), nominaliser, inchoative/factitive/causative/reflexive-reciprocal derivation are all suffixes ("derivational suffixes which come between the stem and inflectional suffix", §7.1 p. 60), subject/object pronominals are second-position enclitics (§9.2), and the only prefixes are a few derivational/compounding verb prefixes (transport-applicative ray-~yay-, comitative baḏa-, mala- 'together'), which Heath contrasts with "the adjacent prefixing languages" (p. 1) and attributes in part to "diffusional pressures on Ritharngu from prefixing languages like Ngandi and Rembarrnga" (§1.4 p. 6).

It states the same distribution the entry codes, in morphological terms: stress on the Layer-I (primary) case ending of declinable words, on the last stem syllable under a zero ending, on the verbal ending but not the invariant tense marker (or on the stem in the 2sg imperative), final in indeclinables; loans keep stem stress in the direct form and move stress to the Layer-I ending when declined; native adjectives stress the case affix. No procedure, corpus or measurement is described and no source is cited for the stress statement.

301.prule: Main accent on the penultimate syllable of di- and trisyllabic stem words and their derivations ('steeds op de vóór-laatste lettergreep'); on the final syllable in all derivations of monosyllabic stems, in compounds whose last member is a monosyllable (peta-bá, lima-lè) and in a few di-/trisyllabic base words (palák, kaifú, kaifòk, kelumèk). No stress shift under affixation.
301.srule: One weaker accent (neven-accent) in words of more than three syllables, on the 4th syllable from the end (3rd from the end when the main stress is final), i.e. two syllables before the main stress: luü-eik (lu), kelumèk (ke) — 'een dubbel accent', two accents per word, not an iterating alternation. Living prefixes never carry it (napadeik, manapadeik have a single accent); in words ending in a reduplicated form it stands further left (kaki-uüle, kai-lilí); a monosyllabic first member of a compound carries it (pa-bafi); equally the first syllable of trisyllabic base words with penult stress and of disyllabic base words with final stress carries a neven-accent and is relatively long (sikou, tekauk, kobusuk, solá, tupè, p. 6), but not when that first syllable has the vowel a, which is felt as the prefix pa- and is not long (palák), nor in some loanwords with another vowel (selaka, silaka).

corr.detail: The database's own quoted passage (Hayes 1995:199) puts secondary stress on odd-numbered NON-final syllables, and Bye 2001:109-111 foots three-syllable words as (σσ)σ, leaving the final syllable unstressed. 303.dq: Stress is assigned by constructing syllabic trochees from left to right (Bye 1997b). Main stress is on the initial syllable (196). ... It thus approximates to the notion foot, except that a stress group is not necessarily binary, and may include the final syllable of an imparisyllabic word. 303.sec_rule: Secondary stress on the head of each non-initial syllabic trochee built left to right, i.e. on the 3rd, 5th, 7th... syllables; feet are strictly binary, so the final syllable of a word with an odd number of syllables is unfooted and unstressed: (véah.ke).hih, (át.tes).(tèas.tiih), (mĕáh:tse).(tàa.luj).(ðà.sa).meh.
303.sec_quote: b. (véah.ke).hih 'to assist' c. (át.tes).(tèas.tiih) 'to give a tiny bit' d. (mĕáh:tse).(tàa.luj).(ðà.sa).meh 'to our forest farms' e. (ráh:kaa).(sèa.meh) 'our beloved' ... A trisyllabic word is taken here to be footed as (σσ)σ, i.e. the final syllable is not part of the foot. ... In trisyllabic words, the third and final syllable is unstressed.

305.dq: Stress is very largely predictable in San, falling on the penultimate syllable except when the final syllable is əʔ, in which case it falls on the third-last syllable, e.g. líkudəʔ back
305.dloc: Sneddon 1984:20 §2.1.1.2 (PL B-91 PDF in the copy consulted); §2.1.6 p.25: "this syllable does not take or influence stress, the preceding syllable acting as the word-final syllable for the purpose of stress placement"; StressTyp2 entry (same statement) and words ˈbale, baˈleku, ˈlikudəʔ
305.prule: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable; the paragogic final syllable əʔ (added after final consonants other than ŋ and ʔ) does not count, so words ending in əʔ are stressed on the third-last syllable (líkudəʔ, úhasəʔ); a penult containing ə is stressed like any other (tə́lu).
305.srule: Not mentioned in Sneddon 1984 (PL B-91), secs. 2.1.1.2 p.20, 2.1.6 p.25, 2.3.23 p.53 read: the San stress section is a single sentence on primary (penultimate) stress and says nothing about secondary or rhythmic stress.
305.quote: 2.1.1.2. Stress. Stress is very largely predictable in San, falling on the penultimate syllable except when the final syllable is əʔ, in which case it falls on the third-last syllable, e.g. líkudəʔ back (see section 2.1.6. for a discussion of final syllable əʔ). [p.25 sec.2.1.6] this syllable does not take or influence stress, the preceding syllable acting as the word-final syllable for the purpose of stress placement. [p.53 sec.2.3.23] Word stress is predictable in San, falling on the penult (not counting the paragoge) even if this contains ə (see section 2.1.1.2.).

morph.elicq: Introduction, 'Procedure in analysis', p.iv: "This grammar was prepared inductively. Rather than using an informant from whom utterances were elicited and then experimented with by further elicitation, we used the corpus which was selected from the tape-recorded texts and letters. ... The entire corpus consisted of about 300 tape-recorded texts, which represent about 40 hours of listening time, in addition to 250 letters". The stress examples in §3.30 are all cited from recorded texts (N81, C8, I9, A21, A8, I55), e.g. ex.1 '-N81', and §8.12.10 notes of pepe 'on magnetic tape it sounds as if...'. morph.stmt: Sango is almost entirely isolating: "The verbs of Sango, like the other classes of words, are morphologically quite simple. Their only affix is a- which marks the subject (q.v. 7.20). Otherwise, there is no inflection for any grammatical category whatsoever" (§9.10 p.156); on nouns "Except for the category of plural number, which is marked by the prefix â-, no other semantic or grammatical category is represented with the noun itself" (§6.10 p.127) and "Derivation of nouns is achieved only by the suffixation of verbs with -ngô" (§6.20) — i.e. two prefixes (subject marker a-, plural â-) and one suffix (nominalizer -ngô), everything else by free particles/connectives, mostly postposed…

tn.quote: 1.31. There are three phonemic tones in Sango, high, mid, and low. For reasons given below mid is not symbolized, but high tone is marked by the diacritic (') and low tone is left unmarked. There are glides from low to a higher level and from high to a lower level. These are represented as sequences of low-high and high-low respectively. ... 1.33. Mid tone (i.e. one which is between high and low in a given environment) is a marginal phoneme in Sango. In only five words does it contrast with high and low tones in an identical tonal frame.

306.cfw: Samarin's grammar (1963, published 1967), the only first-hand description of Sango stress, says stress is not phonemic and only sometimes occurs for expressive effect, falling on the first syllable when it does, and his 1967 Basic Course tells learners not to stress any syllable, so the fixed-initial label taken over from Gordon 2002 and StressTyp2 (Goedemans, Heinz & van der Hulst 2015) captures the placement but overstates the type, while Jacquot 1960 treats Bangui Sango purely as a three-tone language and says nothing about stress.

corr.head: StressTyp2 codes a fixed pattern that its source does not state
corr.detail: StressTyp2 codes initial primary stress; the descriptions on record conflict (Bodding 1929: no fixed positional rule, quantity decides; Ghosh 2008: fixed second-syllable stress) and neither states initial stress. The language is therefore not listed under fixed stress.

contra.head: The published descriptions contradict each other
contra.detail: Ghosh 2008 (§2.5 p. 30, repeated §2.6 p. 31) states fixed second-syllable stress irrespective of syllable type; Bodding 1929 (§155 p. 133, §157 pp. 133-134) states that there is no fixed general rule for the place of stress, that quantity always makes itself felt, and that disyllables may be stressed on either syllable. Neukom 2001: 8, as quoted by Horo & Anderson 2021: 298 (not read directly), gives a third account for disyllabic stems: stress on the first syllable unless the first syllable is light and the second heavy, in which case the second syllable is stressed. No positional rule is adopted while the descriptions conflict.

307.srule: Bodding 1929: words of three or more syllables (and some disyllables) split into 'stress-units' of at most two syllables, each carrying its own stress, near-level, with a weaker unit marked by a low stroke (e.g.,bebe'nao, a'nar,go, mu,nu'cat', 'parga'na, 'kar'bari,a); reduplicated/infixed trisyllables carry the heavier stress on the ultima; in k'-infixed trisyllables the stress generally falls on the vowel immediately before the k' (only a couple of words with an initial nasalized vowel and a few with an initial diphthong keep the principal stress in its original place and add an 'anticipating' stress before the k'; penult-stressed trisyllables likewise get an anticipating stress on the vowel before the k', provided two stress-units are not formed); the stress inside each unit follows the disyllable quantity/lexical rules, so the minor stresses have no fixed rhythmic position. Modern sources (Neukom 2001:8 via Horo & Anderson 2021, Ghosh 2008, Horo & Anderson 2021) do not mention secondary stress.

morph.stmt: Ghosh 2008 p.11: 'Santali is a Munda language with a suffixing, agglutinating, and a basic SOV structure'; verb template per Neukom 2000 (2): 'stem + TAM + pronoun (DO or dative) (+IPFV) + POSS + pronoun (possessor) + FIN + pronoun (subject)' — all inflection is post-root (suffixes and enclitics, the subject enclitic often landing on the word before the verb), the only pre-root material being an unproductive nominalising prefix ma- and a lexicalised causative a- in a few verbs, while much lexical derivation (nominalisation, reciprocal, some causatives/plurals) is by root-internal infixes.

side_1.quote: Stress is always on the second syllable of a word unless it is monosyllabic, irrespective of whether it is an open or a closed syllable.

side_2.quote: 155. There is in the language no fixed general rule for where stress is to be applied, whether on the first or on the last syllable of a word (or unit) or elsewhere. The stress may be anywhere, only that in the same word it will remain in the same place [...] 157. [...] quantity and stress are intimately connected in Santali, quantity always making itself felt. [...] (c) Dissyllabic words may…

conflict.would_settle: (a) Reading Neukom 2001 Santali (LW/M 323) p.8 and its phonology chapter directly (bibliography row 4; no open copy, print at Harvard Widener PL4563.1.N48 2001x) to see his data basis and what he says of tri-/polysyllables - a third modern first-hand leg; (b) Horo & Anderson 2022 'A preliminary study on prominence in Assam Santali disyllables' (Deccan College volume, print only, bibliography row 11) and their announced follow-up on inflected/polysyllabic words; decisively (c) an instrumental study of heavy-initial disyllables ('dangra, 'sarjom type) and trisyllables in a core-region lect (Santal Parganas / West Bengal), which would test Bodding's quantity rule against Ghosh's quantity-insensitive second-syllable rule on the same variety. Anderson 2006 (ELL2 'Santali', paywalled, row 10) would show which description the field's standard reference adopts but would not by itself break the tie.

307.cfw: Bodding 1929 finds no general rule and treats Santali stress as fixed word by word, Neukom 2001 describes weight-sensitive stress with an initial default, and Ghosh 2008 together with the instrumental study of Assam Santali disyllables by Horo and Anderson 2021 put stress on the second syllable, so the type of system is still openly contested and the catalog leaves it undetermined.

308.prule: Length-conditioned fixed stress: words of two and three syllables are stressed on the first syllable, and in words of more than three syllables primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable with secondary stress on the word-initial syllable (Borgman 1990:222: 'au.lu 'wounded, sick', 'i.po.ko 'wind', 'ka.pu.''lu.mö 'yam', 'ho.ko.''na.to 'type of vine', 'mö.ta.ti.''le.mö 'a type of banana').
308.srule: Secondary stress on the word-initial syllable in words of more than three syllables (Borgman 1990:222: 'with secondary stress word intial:... 'ka.pu.''lu.mö, 'ho.ko.''na.to, 'mö.ta.ti.''le.mö').
308.quote: Stress is on the first syllable of two-syllable and three-syllable words; in words of more than three syllables, primary stress is on the penultimate syllable, with secondary stress word intial: 'au.lu 'wounded, sick'; 'na.kö 'tooth'; 'i.po.ko 'wind'; 'ha.no.ko 'ax'; 'to.lo.ko 'crooked'; 'ka.pu.''lu.mö 'yam'; 'ho.ko.''na.to a 'type of vine'; 'mö.ta.ti.''le.mö 'a type of banana'.

evidence_works.detail: Stress falls on the main (final) syllable; the presyllable is unstressed; words are at most bisyllabic apart from one trisyllabic derivative with the affix lo- (p. 32). No secondary stress mentioned; no weight condition stated. Tone: none; the vowel contrast is a two-way register (tense = laryngealized/creaky vs lax = clear), described 'only by the feature of voice quality'; 'Consonant voicing, pitch, and vowel harmony... do not pertain to the Sedang situation' (p. 49). 'Vietnamese tone' (index, p. 80) concerns loans, not Sedang. The catalog entry cites Smith 1979 (Pacific Linguistics B-50)

morph.stmt: Selepet is almost exclusively suffixing/encliticising: "There are only two word classes in Selepet: the noun and the verb. These differ from each other in the filler classes manifesting the nuclei and their suffixal morphology" (B-21 p.63); the verb "has the suffixal structure" +nucleus ±benefactive +mode +tense +person-number (Table A), nouns are +nucleus +number +possession (§3.1.1), case relators are enclitics, particles are free roots, stem-level constructions or enclitics (§1.4.8), and the only prefixes in the language are the object markers of the single verb root -n 'to call someone', which "are clearly prefixal" (p.38).

313.prule: Stress always falls on the word-final syllable, which is an obligatory heavy (major) syllable; non-final syllables, whether minor or major, are unstressed (one foot at the right edge of the prosodic word).

313.quote: The major syllable has at least five properties. 313.exc_quote: [Miyakoshi 2006 p.77 fn. 29] 29) Since stress usually falls only on the word-final position in the Aslian languages, I here assume tentatively that it does when the heavy syllable is reduplicated, too. If stress turns out to fall on both the base and the reduplicant, then they would each constitute a prosodic word, and the following structure would be optimal where the base as well as the reduplicant is footed: (d_.ynp:l)-(ynp:l). 317.prule: Stress falls on the initial syllable of the lexical root ('In the majority of lexical roots (including all verbs) the initial syllable is stressed', p. 7); affixes, clitics and most grammatical morphemes are unstressed, so in unprefixed words stress is word-initial. 'A number of roots' (nouns; no verbs) have an unstressed initial syllable and medial stress, e.g. sika [si'ka] 'goat', kàlaga [ka'lara], and loans such as bútùng 'bottle', dogotáró 'doctor' (pp. 7, 36, 46-47, 50).
317.srule: None in simple words: 'In general there is one stressed syllable per lexical root'; affixes and clitics in general 'do not have stress' (one exception: 'the stressed suffix -ŋkaN-' of manner nominalizations, p. 113). Two-root compounds carry two stresses: 'Roots usually keep their stress in compounds, so that a two-root compound will have two stressed syllables' (not ranked primary/secondary).

morph.elicq: No statement of how stress was determined; the grammar's evidence base in general is a text corpus: "... examples used are taken from the text collection alluded to in section 1.5 above. Occasionally elicited examples are used in the interests of clarity." (Carlson 1994 ch.1, snippets data2/data4). The stress diagnostics Carlson gives are distributional/segmental (root-initial position; [d] in stressed vs flap [r] in unstressed non-initial syllables; vowel harmony and high-vowel elision in unstressed syllables), not instrumental.

vlen.q: There are no closed syllables in Supyire. Syllables are basically CV or CVV. A few grammatical words (e.g. the pronouns u and uru) begin with a V syllable. Only one kind of consonant cluster occurs: nasal + stop.

tn.quote: There are four phonemic tones. The high (H) and low (L) are fairly ordinary, but the middle two are differentiated in behavior rather than pitch. One of these, which we will call strong mid (Ms) undergoes substantially less perturbation than the other, which we will call weak mid (Mw). As will become apparent, weak mid resembles high in its behavior. Northern Senufo languages (Supyire, Sucite, Mamara) all have both weak and strong mid tones. Central Senufo languages such as Cebaara and Shenara, however, seem to have a more conventional three tone-system.
tn.cite: Carlson, Robert. 1994. A Grammar of Supyire (Mouton Grammar Library 14). Berlin/New York: Mouton de Gruyter

tn.note: Four level tones H, Ms, Mw, L (the two mids share a pitch, differ under tone rules); roots carry tunes linked to the stressed vowel; stress separate, root-initial; H downstep by rule; floating L. A second reading (Carlson 1983): Three level tones, high, mid and low; successive highs are automatically downstepped (H H -> H 'H, with 'H at mid pitch) and mid and high downdrift after low; a mid-raising rule keeps H and M apart. Checked against the source (tone consistency check, 2026-09-23): tone-bearing unit syllable -> unstated (Carlson 1994 pp. 42-43, ch. 2 sec. 2.3 Tone, paragraph after the four-tone …).
